justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modestly bullish baseline for what appears to be an asset trading around the 364–365 range. For the 1-day horizon, I anchored closely to the last observed price, assuming mean-reverting intraday dynamics with minimal directional drift — hence the 364.5 estimate. For the 1-week horizon, I applied a slight upward drift of roughly 0.4%, reflecting a modest positive trend assumption consistent with recent momentum without overweighting any single directional signal. For the 1-month horizon, I extended that drift further to 370, implying roughly 1.5% appreciation, which is consistent with a moderate bull case but intentionally conservative to avoid overconfidence in trend persistence over a longer horizon.

The confidence interval widths were calibrated to reflect increasing uncertainty at longer time horizons, as is standard in time-series forecasting. At 1 day, the 21-point range (354–375) captures typical daily volatility, roughly ±3% around the point estimate. At 1 week, the range widens to 36 points, reflecting the compounding of daily uncertainty and the possibility of a meaningful directional move developing. At 1 month, the 70-point range acknowledges that macro conditions, sentiment shifts, and fundamental repricing can all accumulate meaningfully over four weeks.

Several specific risks could push outcomes outside these intervals. On the downside, a sudden macro shock — such as an unexpected central bank policy shift, a deterioration in risk sentiment, or a negative earnings or economic data surprise — could push prices well below the lower bound of my 1-month interval of 335. Liquidity events or correlated asset selloffs could amplify moves beyond what historical volatility alone would suggest. On the upside, a strong positive catalyst such as better-than-expected economic data, a policy pivot, or a short-squeeze dynamic could drive prices above 405 for the 1-month horizon.

It is also worth noting that my intervals, being 90% confidence intervals, are explicitly designed to be violated roughly 10% of the time under the assumed model. In practice, financial returns tend to have fat tails, meaning the true probability of an extreme outcome is likely slightly higher than the 5% I've assigned to each tail. Structural breaks, geopolitical events, or idiosyncratic news specific to this asset could all generate tail outcomes that no probabilistic model fully anticipates.
